To shove means to push someone or something with force and roughness. It is never gentle. The action is quick, strong, and often careless or aggressive.

Think of "push" as a broad word that can describe anything from gently pressing a button to forcefully moving a boulder. Shove lives only at the rough, forceful end of that scale. If you can imagine someone doing it politely and softly, it's a push — not a shove.
What Exactly Happens When You Shove

When you shove something or someone:

  • You apply sudden, significant force, usually with your hands, arms, shoulder, or body.
  • The thing or person being shoved moves — often stumbles, slides, or gets pushed out of the way.
  • The action often carries a sense of impatience, urgency, or aggression. Even when it isn't meant aggressively, it's still physically rough.

1. Shoving a person

This is when you push someone physically in a rough or forceful way.

  • He shoved the boy against the wall.
  • She was shoved from behind and nearly fell.
  • They were shoving each other to get to the front of the crowd.

Here, shove implies something unpleasant — it's the kind of contact that makes the other person stumble, lose balance, or feel threatened. It's the word you'd use in a street fight, a crowd crush, or a moment of anger.

2. Shoving objects

This is when you force an object into a place, often quickly and without much care.

  • He shoved his clothes into the bag and ran for the door.
  • She shoved the report under her desk when her boss walked in.
  • He shoved the broken chair into the corner.

Notice the feeling here: there's no careful arrangement, no delicacy — just a quick, forceful stuffing or pushing of something somewhere. This is very common in everyday language and doesn't involve anger — just hurry or carelessness.

This is what separates shove from similar words, and it's important.

Shove always implies roughness. Even in casual, non-angry use (like shoving socks into a drawer), the word signals that the action was forceful and without finesse.

When used on a person, shove almost always has a negative or hostile tone. It is the word used when someone is being rude, aggressive, impatient, or physically threatening. If someone says "he pushed me," it could have been accidental. If someone says "he shoved me," it feels deliberate and forceful.

Compare:

  • She pushed the door open. → Neutral. Could have been gentle.
  • She shoved the door open. → Forceful. She clearly put her weight into it. There's energy and roughness here.
Shove Used Without a Specific Target

Sometimes shove is used to describe general rough physical movement:

  • People were shoving at the concert. (pushing each other roughly)
  • Stop shoving! (stop pushing people around you)
  • He elbowed and shoved his way through the crowd. (he forced his way through, using his body to push people aside)

"Shove off" — An informal, rude way to tell someone to go away or leave.
"Shove off, I'm busy." = "Get lost. Leave me alone."

"Shove it" (or "you can shove it") — A very rude, offensive expression used to reject something with contempt, essentially meaning "I want nothing to do with this." Often used when someone is furiously refusing an offer, a job, or an instruction.
"He told his boss to shove the job." = He quit angrily and disrespectfully.

"If push comes to shove" — This is a fixed idiom (a set phrase) that means: if the situation becomes really serious or critical and you are forced to act. It describes a point where a problem can no longer be avoided.
"I'd prefer to solve this peacefully, but if push comes to shove, we'll take legal action."

Note: This phrase uses both "push" and "shove" to suggest an escalation — from pushing to shoving — as a metaphor for things getting more serious.
How Shove Compares to Similar Words

Understanding where shove sits among similar words will sharpen your feel for it.

  • Nudge → Very gentle, usually deliberate. You nudge someone with your elbow to quietly get their attention. Soft and subtle.
  • Push → Neutral. Can be gentle or forceful. No strong emotional signal.
  • Shove → Always forceful, always rough. Often implies rudeness, haste, or aggression.
  • Thrust → Forceful and very directional — a sharp, pointed action forward or in a specific direction. A knife is thrust; a sword is thrust.
  • Jostle → Bumping and pushing in a crowd, often unintentionally or as part of movement. Less aggressive than shove, more chaotic.

To shove is to push with force and roughness — whether you're pushing a person (usually aggressively or rudely) or cramming an object somewhere quickly (usually out of haste or carelessness). The word always carries the feeling of more force than necessary, making it rougher, ruder, or more urgent than a simple push.
